== EXTRACTION RULES (GEMINI_HANDOFF_BRIEF §3 Task C & §5.2; CODEBOOK.md §§1-9; RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1) ==
1. ACCESSIBILITY GATE:

NEVER copy publication year or country from the citation header when the full paper was not read!
2. IF FULL TEXT IS READABLE:
   - Extract each of the 9 fields strictly from the paper text. Write a field value ONLY if the paper explicitly states it; if not stated in the paper, write `"not reported"` in `value` and explain in `comment`. Never guess or infer from context.
   - `publication_year`: 4-digit year printed on the paper/report itself (e.g. `"2024"`), or `"not reported"` if undated. Give exact page/header in `where_found`.
   - `country`: Country or countries studied as stated in the paper (use semicolon-separated names if multiple specific countries, or exact global/regional scope as stated, e.g. `"Global (48 countries)"`), or `"not reported"`.
   - `sample_size`: Exact sample size(s) AND explicit unit(s) of analysis stated in the paper (e.g. `"593 households across 4 neighbourhoods"`, `"128 municipalities; 2,048 observations (2010-2025)"`, `"32 semi-structured interviews"`), or `"not reported"` if pure doctrinal/legal analysis with no empirical sample.
   - `study_design`: Study design as the authors describe it and as operationalized in the methods section (be specific about quantitative/qualitative/quasi-experimental/experimental/review structure).
   - `effect_estimate`: Headline result of the study regarding how the legal, administrative, regulatory, institutional, tenure, tariff/subsidy, or participation factor relates to water/sanitation access/outcomes, with exact printed numbers (point estimates, units, 95% CIs, p-values, sample N) if quantitative, or concise factual headline finding if qualitative (noting `"Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported"` when purely qualitative), in your own words from the paper alone.
   - `risk_of_bias_tool`: Pick the single design-matched tool per `RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1:
     * `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"` (individually randomized trial)
     * `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"` (cluster-randomized trial — check unit of randomization carefully!)
     * `"ROBINS-I"` (non-randomized intervention / quasi-experimental study with a genuine comparator: DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, policy panel FE)
     * `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"` (quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without quasi-experimental intervention comparator)
     * `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"` (observational longitudinal cohort study without intervention framing)
     * `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"` (primary qualitative study: interviews, focus groups, ethnography, qualitative case study)
     * `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"` (genuine mixed-methods study combining both qualitative and quantitative primary components)
     * `"AMSTAR 2"` (systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with systematic search/screening; NEVER use for non-systematic narrative literature reviews)
     * `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"` (legal-empirical, doctrinal-empirical, jurimetric, or institutional-historical study that fits none of the six conventional designs above)
     * `"NONE"` (fits none of the listed tools, e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model, or non-systematic narrative review/essay without primary empirical data or systematic search — explain why in `comment`)
   - `mechanism_certainty`: Single integer `"0"`, `"1"`, `"2"`, `"3"`, or `"4"` strictly obeying `CODEBOOK.md` §9 and its design ceiling:
     * `"4"` ONLY for randomized trials (`RoB 2`)
     * `"3"` ONLY for `RoB 2` trials OR `ROBINS-I` studies with credible Low/Moderate overall risk of bias
     * All other designs (cross-sectional/JBI, cohort, qualitative/CASP, mixed-methods/MMAT, systematic review/AMSTAR 2, Legal Framework, NONE, or Serious/Critical ROBINS-I) CANNOT exceed `"2"`! (`"2"` = mechanism directly observed empirically; `"1"` = documented statistical/descriptive association; `"0"` = inferred only by authors).
   - `outcome_flags`: Comma-separated list using ONLY exact `CODEBOOK.md` §5 codes actually studied in the paper (`formal_connection`, `water_access`, `sanitation_access`, `service_coverage`, `service_reliability`, `service_quantity`, `service_quality`, `affordability`, `service_continuity`, `application_success`, `refusal`, `delay`), or `"not reported"`.
   - `mechanism_flags`: Comma-separated list of applicable top-level family codes (`ELIGIBILITY`, `BURDEN`, `DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION`, `ENFORCEMENT`) followed by exact detailed `CODEBOOK.md` §4 codes actually studied in the paper (`documentation`, `tenure`, `property`, `planning`, `zoning`, `building_permit`, `service_area`, `fees`, `procedural_steps`, `delay`, `discretion`, `hardship_exception`, `accommodation`, `administrative_review`, `complaint`, `judicial_review`, `disconnection`, `reconnection`, `sanction`, `participation`, `institutional_fragmentation`, `political_coordination`, `bureaucratic_assistance`), or `"not reported"`.

evidence_quotes.quote: Semi-structured interviews with 24 street vendors in the central area
Six public managers were also interviewed, two from the Secretariat
Although Brazil supported the Human Rights to Water and Sanitation (HRWS) Resolution in 2010, these rights are not explicitly recognized in the country’s National
While public managers often expressed support for HRWS in public discourse, this recognition is rarely reflected in actual practice.
Institutional - Ensuring water and sanitation access for street vendors in Brazil is further hindered by weak cross–sectoral coordination.
These relationships—based on trust, reciprocity, or small payments—allow vendors to use facilities like toilets or water taps.

country.comment: Single-city empirical study conducted in the municipality of Juiz de Fora, state of Minas Gerais, Brazil.
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Title & Abstract; PDF p. 2, Section 2; PDF p. 3, Section 3.1

effect_estimate.comment: Purely qualitative study; descriptive contextual costs (e.g., ~US$0.50 private toilet fee, ~US$3,200/month CESAMA operating support, ~US$35,000 network extension cost) and inter-coder reliability metrics (>80% agreement, Krippendorff's alpha >0.8) are reported, with no quantitative effect estimates.
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported. Statutory definitions in national and municipal sanitation laws (Federal Law No. 11.445/2007; Juiz de Fora Law No. 14.290/2020) frame service universalization around occupied households and building connections, excluding public spaces from the 2022 Municipal Water and Sanitation Plan and from the municipal utility's (CESAMA) perceived operational mandate under Law No. 13.303/2016. Combined with weak cross-sectoral coordination across municipal secretariats, lack of accountability, slow procurement bidding for basic maintenance, heritage/environmental/land-ownership embargoes (halting the Halfeld Park toilet renovation for two years and delaying the Alma Lavada container toilet startup by more than a year), and political discontinuity, public water and toilet provision in downtown Juiz de Fora remains ad hoc and inadequate, leaving informal street vendors reliant on self-improvisation ("sevirologia"), favors from formal businesses, or paid private toilets (~US$0.50 per use).
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF pp. 4-8, Sections 3.1-3.3 & Section 4, Table 1

mechanism_certainty.comment: Rated 2 (mechanism directly observed) respecting the design ceiling of 2 for a primary qualitative study appraised with the CASP Qualitative Checklist. Interviews and municipal legal/administrative records directly document how household-bound statutory definitions, state-enterprise mandate restrictions, inter-departmental permitting/heritage embargoes, and procurement bureaucracy restrict public water and toilet provision for street vendors.

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines statutory household/building-connection scope exclusions (service_area), omission from municipal sanitation plans and heritage planning embargoes (planning), land-ownership permitting objections (property), private toilet use charges and municipal vending fees (fees), procurement tendering rules for minor repairs (procedural_steps), >1-year implementation/utility-connection and 2-year renovation delays (delay), managers' statutory interpretations and SEDH bypassing inter-departmental authorization (discretion), split mandates across SEPUR/CESAMA/SESMAUR/SEDH/DEMLURB/CONPUR (institutional_fragmentation), and weak cross-sector coordination plus partisan discontinuity (political_coordination).
mechanism_flags.value: ELIGIBILITY, BURDEN, DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION, service_area, planning, property, fees, procedural_steps, delay, discretion, institutional_fragmentation, political_coordination

outcome_flags.comment: Examines street vendors' access to drinking fountains/water points (water_access) and public toilets (sanitation_access), out-of-pocket fees of ~US$0.50 per toilet use (affordability), hygiene/cleanliness/water-pressure/accessibility defects (service_quality), facility closures, daytime-only operating hours (9 a.m.-6 p.m.), and political discontinuation risks (service_continuity), and multi-year renovation/startup and maintenance procurement delays (delay).
outcome_flags.value: water_access, sanitation_access, affordability, service_quality, service_continuity, delay

publication_year.comment: Published in Utilities Policy Volume 97 (2025), article 102051; accepted 4 September 2025 and available online 11 September 2025.

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Primary qualitative study employing focused ethnography, snowball-sampled semi-structured interviews, and qualitative content analysis; matched to CASP Qualitative Checklist per RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1.

sample_size.comment: Snowball sample reaching theoretical saturation; municipal records also note a background population of 123 fixed street vending spots and an estimated 459 informal workers in downtown Juiz de Fora (cited from Moreira, 2025). Public managers interviewed comprised 2 from SEPUR, 1 from CESAMA, 1 from SESMAUR, and 2 from SEDH.
sample_size.value: 30 semi-structured interviews (24 informal street vendors and 6 municipal public managers in Juiz de Fora)

study_design.comment: Focused ethnography conducted in downtown Juiz de Fora with non-probabilistic snowball sampling up to theoretical saturation and double-coded qualitative content analysis (Schreier, 2012), combined with analysis of municipal sanitation laws, plans, and utility bylaws.
study_design.value: Qualitative focused ethnography (2021-2023) using snowball-sampled semi-structured interviews and qualitative content analysis, supplemented by municipal policy and legal document analysis
study_design.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF pp. 2-3, Section 2; PDF p. 5, Section 3.2.1
